saint_pick.name: Lorcán Ua Tuathail
saint_pick.selection_reason: Laurence O'Toole has the strongest Catholic sourcing (Catholic Encyclopedia, Santi e Beati, Ökumenisches Heiligenlexikon) and a vivid, well-documented life: a hostage boy, an abbot who fed the starving, the archbishop of Dublin who tried to broker peace during the Norman invasion and died in exile at Eu, and a heart relic that was stolen and then recovered. It also gives Ireland and the 12th century, which breaks the run of Italian and Central European saints.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Canonized by Pope Honorius III in 1225; listed in the Roman Martyrology on November 14, his dies natalis, and kept as a feast in the liturgical calendars of Ireland, including the Archdiocese of Dublin.

beats.text: Laurence O'Toole was born around eleven twenty-eight in Leinster, Ireland, a chieftain's son.
He entered the monastic school at Glendalough and studied there thirteen years. Then the monks unanimously chose him as abbot.
beats.scene: A young monk in a dark habit stands among his brothers in the green Glendalough valley, with a tall stone round tower, a small stone church and wooded hills behind them, as the community gathers around him.

beats.text: The old Lives say that in a famine, he gave the monastery's goods to the hungry.
beats.scene: An abbot in a monastic habit stands at a monastery gate handing loaves from baskets to a crowd of thin, ragged men, women and children in medieval Irish dress, with stone monastery buildings behind him.

beats.text: In eleven sixty-two he became Archbishop of Dublin, the first Irishman in that see. Beneath his robes he wore a hair shirt. Each year he withdrew forty days to Saint Kevin's cave.
beats.scene: A bishop in a mitre and rich vestments, holding a crozier, stands in the Romanesque stone Christ Church cathedral of Dublin, with clergy in white around him and candlelight on the arches.

beats.text: When King Henry the Second came, Laurence worked for peace between the kings. He followed Henry across the sea to plead for King Roderic. He died in Normandy in eleven eighty, far from home.
beats.scene: An aged bishop lies on a simple bed in a stone abbey infirmary in Normandy, while Augustinian canons in black habits kneel and tend him by candlelight.

beats.text: Peace is worth the long road. Saint Laurence O'Toole, pray for us.

claims.claim: As a boy of about ten he was taken as a hostage by Dermot McMurrogh, King of Leinster.
He was born about 1128 in what is now County Kildare, the son of a chieftain of Hy Murray, and his mother was of the O'Byrne clan.
He entered the monastic school at Glendalough and studied there for thirteen years.
On the death of Abbot Dunlaing in early 1154, the community unanimously called him to be abbot.
Biographical Lives say that during a famine he gave away the monastery's goods to relieve the hungry.
He was chosen Archbishop of Dublin after Gregory's death in 1161 and was consecrated early in 1162; he was a native-born Irishman, the first Irish-born archbishop of the see.
He wore a hair shirt under his episcopal dress and made an annual forty-day retreat to Saint Kevin's cave near Glendalough.
He converted the secular canons of Christ Church cathedral into Aroasian canons in 1163.
He worked to mediate between the Irish rulers and King Henry II of England, and took part in the Treaty of Windsor in 1175 on behalf of King Roderic of Connacht.
He attended the Third Lateran Council in 1179 and returned as papal legate for Ireland.
In 1179 he crossed to England and then followed King Henry to Normandy to plead the cause of King Roderic.
He died on 14 November 1180 at Eu in Normandy, tended by Abbot Osbert and the canons.
The Roman Martyrology commemorates him on 14 November as a bishop who promoted Church discipline and died while travelling to King Henry.
Pope Honorius III canonized him in 1225.
He is venerated as patron of the city and archdiocese of Dublin.
According to one account, Dermot took him hostage after killing his grandfather, and he was released after his father captured twelve men of the king's retinue.

story: Lorcán Ua Tuathail, known in English as Laurence O'Toole, was born around 1128 in what is now County Kildare, in the kingdom of Leinster. His father was a chieftain of Hy Murray, and his mother belonged to the O'Byrne clan. He was born into a noble family in a restless age, when Irish kings and lineages struggled for power.

When he was about ten, Dermot McMurrogh, King of Leinster, took him as a hostage. Hostages were a common feature of medieval Irish politics, a way of guaranteeing agreements between rival chiefs. One later account says the king had killed the boy's grandfather and that the boy was freed only after his father captured twelve men from the king's company. The details come mostly from the old biographical tradition, but the hostage childhood itself is part of every account.

In 1140 the boy obtained permission to enter the monastic school of Glendalough, in the Wicklow hills. The valley was a sanctuary, founded long before by Saint Kevin, a center of worship, teaching and monastic life. Laurence studied there for thirteen years and became known for his piety and learning. When Abbot Dunlaing died in early 1154, the community called him unanimously to take his place. He was still a young man.

The old Lives remember him as an abbot of both authority and charity. Tradition holds that during a famine he gave away the monastery's goods to feed the hungry. We cannot verify every detail of such stories, but they show what people remembered of him: a man who treated the goods of the Church as belonging to the poor. He declined the bishopric of Glendalough in 1160 out of humility.

In 1161 Gregory, Archbishop of Dublin, died, and Laurence was chosen to succeed him. He was consecrated early in 1162 at Christ Church cathedral by Gilla Isu, Primate of Armagh. He was the first native Irishman to hold the see. The city had been a Scandinavian port, and its bishops had looked to Canterbury. His appointment marked a new chapter. He set about reform, turning the canons of Christ Church into a community living under a common rule in 1163. He supported the foundation of All Hallows priory a few years later.

He did not ask of others what he would not do himself. Beneath his episcopal vestments he wore a hair shirt, and every year he retired for forty days to Saint Kevin's cave near Glendalough. The Lives also remember his care for the poor, the sick and children left without support. Any numbers handed down cannot be treated as figures from a register, but they speak of a bishop whose charity was well known.

His years in Dublin coincided with the Norman arrival. From 1169 warriors from the Anglo-Norman world came to Leinster, and Dublin was taken in 1170. Laurence was an Irish nobleman and also the shepherd of a contested city. Tradition says he tried to negotiate peace before the city fell and helped the victims afterward. When Henry II came to Ireland, Laurence treated him with due respect and worked as a go-between. He took part in the Treaty of Windsor in 1175, which sought to define the spheres of Henry and Roderic, King of Connacht. In 1178 he received Cardinal Vivian, the papal legate, at the Synod of Dublin. In 1179 he attended the Third Lateran Council, where he was named papal legate for Ireland.

His last journey was made for the sake of peace. Moved, as the Catholic Encyclopedia says, by burning charity for King Roderic's cause, he crossed to England in September 1179. He was detained for three weeks at Abingdon Abbey, then followed King Henry to Normandy. At the Augustinian abbey of Eu he fell ill. Abbot Osbert and the canons tended him, and he died there on 14 November 1180. The Roman Martyrology records that he died on the way to King Henry, still working to restore concord among princes.
Devotion grew at his tomb at Eu and in Ireland. Pope Honorius III canonized him in 1225, and his feast is kept on November 14. He is honored as patron of the city and archdiocese of Dublin.

issues: Story paragraph 3 describes Glendalough's 'round tower' and 'churches'. None of the four sources mention these, so the sentence now uses only what they say: a center of worship, teaching and monastic life.

Story paragraph 6 says 'Their numbers cannot be treated as figures from a register', but no numbers are given anywhere in the story. The sentence now reads 'Any numbers handed down...', which matches the Santi e Beati caveat about unverifiable figures.

The spoken beats check out against the sources. They run about 137 words, the hook is 11 words, and the famine story is marked as the 'old Lives say'. The hostage age of ten, the thirteen years at Glendalough, the unanimous election as abbot, the 1162 consecration, the first Irishman in the see, the hair shirt, the forty-day retreat, the mediation, the plea for Roderic and the 1180 death in Normandy are all supported. No change was needed to the beats.
factcheck.reviewer_note: Check the 'who' map pin: it sits on Dublin, but he was born in County Kildare (Castledermot or Kilkea). Dublin is within Leinster and is his see, so it is acceptable. Also, the hook states the hostage-at-ten detail as fact, following the Catholic Encyclopedia; Santi e Beati and the Heiligenlexikon say it rests on biographical tradition and give a slightly later date (about 1141).

es.name: San Lorenzo O'Toole
es.hook: Un muchacho entregado como rehén llegó a ser pastor de Dublín y gastó sus últimas fuerzas en la paz.
es.summary: San Lorenzo O'Toole, abad irlandés del siglo XII y arzobispo de Dublín, fue rehén siendo niño y más tarde entregó su vida a la reforma, la caridad y la paz.
story: Lorcán Ua Tuathail, conocido en inglés como Laurence O'Toole, nació hacia 1128 en lo que hoy es el condado de Kildare, en el reino de Leinster. Su padre era un jefe de Hy Murray y su madre pertenecía al clan O'Byrne. Nació en una familia noble en una época inquieta, cuando los reyes y los linajes irlandeses luchaban por el poder.

Cuando tenía unos diez años, Dermot McMurrogh, rey de Leinster, lo tomó como rehén. Los rehenes eran una práctica común en la política medieval irlandesa, una forma de garantizar los acuerdos entre jefes rivales. Un relato posterior dice que el rey había matado al abuelo del niño y que el muchacho solo fue liberado después de que su padre capturara a doce hombres de la comitiva del rey. Los detalles proceden sobre todo de la antigua tradición biográfica, pero la infancia como rehén forma parte de todos los relatos.

En 1140 el muchacho obtuvo permiso para ingresar en la escuela monástica de Glendalough, en las colinas de Wicklow. El valle era un santuario, fundado mucho antes por San Kevin, un centro de culto, enseñanza y vida monástica. Lorenzo estudió allí durante trece años y se hizo conocido por su piedad y su saber. Cuando el abad Dunlaing murió a comienzos de 1154, la comunidad lo llamó por unanimidad para ocupar su lugar. Todavía era joven.

Las antiguas Vidas lo recuerdan como un abad de autoridad y de caridad. Según la tradición, durante una hambruna repartió los bienes del monasterio para alimentar a los hambrientos. No podemos verificar cada detalle de estas historias, pero muestran lo que la gente recordaba de él: un hombre que trataba los bienes de la Iglesia como pertenecientes a los pobres. En 1160 rechazó el obispado de Glendalough por humildad.

En 1161 murió Gregorio, arzobispo de Dublín, y Lorenzo fue elegido para sucederle. Fue consagrado a comienzos de 1162 en la catedral de Christ Church por Gilla Isu, primado de Armagh. Fue el primer irlandés de nacimiento en ocupar la sede. La ciudad había sido un puerto escandinavo y sus obispos habían mirado hacia Canterbury. Su nombramiento marcó un nuevo capítulo. Emprendió la reforma y, en 1163, convirtió a los canónigos de Christ Church en una comunidad que vivía bajo una regla común. Unos años después apoyó la fundación del priorato de All Hallows.

No pedía a los demás lo que él mismo no haría. Bajo sus vestiduras episcopales llevaba un cilicio, y cada año se retiraba durante cuarenta días a la cueva de San Kevin, cerca de Glendalough. Las Vidas recuerdan también su cuidado de los pobres, de los enfermos y de los niños sin sustento. Las cifras transmitidas no pueden tomarse como datos de un registro, pero hablan de un obispo cuya caridad era muy conocida.

Sus años en Dublín coincidieron con la llegada de los normandos. Desde 1169 llegaron a Leinster guerreros del mundo anglonormando, y Dublín fue tomada en 1170. Lorenzo era un noble irlandés y, al mismo tiempo, el pastor de una ciudad disputada. Según la tradición, intentó negociar la paz antes de que la ciudad cayera y ayudó después a las víctimas. Cuando Enrique II llegó a Irlanda, Lorenzo lo trató con el respeto debido y actuó como intermediario. Participó en el Tratado de Windsor de 1175, que buscaba definir las esferas de Enrique y de Rodrigo, rey de Connacht. En 1178 recibió en el Sínodo de Dublín al cardenal Vivián, legado papal. En 1179 asistió al III Concilio de Letrán, donde fue nombrado legado papal para Irlanda.

Su último viaje lo hizo por la paz. Movido, como dice la Enciclopedia Católica, por una ardiente caridad hacia la causa del rey Rodrigo, cruzó a Inglaterra en septiembre de 1179. Fue retenido durante tres semanas en la abadía de Abingdon y luego siguió al rey Enrique hasta Normandía. En la abadía agustiniana de Eu enfermó. El abad Osberto y los canónigos lo cuidaron, y murió allí el 14 de noviembre de 1180. El Martirologio Romano registra que murió de camino hacia el rey Enrique, aún trabajando por restaurar la concordia entre los príncipes.

La devoción creció en su tumba de Eu y en Irlanda. El papa Honorio III lo canonizó en 1225, y su fiesta se celebra el 14 de noviembre. Es venerado como patrón de la ciudad y de la archidiócesis de Dublín.
es.prayer: La paz vale el largo camino. San Lorenzo O'Toole, ruega por nosotros.
